analysis.title: Global Portfolio Manager's Digest: Clouds of Doubt
key_insights: Neo-cloud credit has repriced sharply on doubts about debt-funded AI infrastructure, but the improvement in credit risk pricing has given stocks little relief. Barclays reads this as concerns about the neo-cloud model being expressed most acutely through equities.
Options markets reinforce the bearish message on neo-clouds. Barclays describes positioning in the group as decidedly bearish.
Barclays credit analysts think CoreWeave's recent weakness was amplified by hedge-fund de-risking and unfavorable press reports.
The stocks that de-rated most are the suppliers of data center inputs. Compute is somewhat commoditized, so neo-clouds are not highly correlated with hyperscalers in price action.

Barclays says the neo-cloud fundamental picture is more resilient than price action implies. It cites a continued supply/demand imbalance for AI infrastructure, a much improved pricing environment, long-term take-or-pay contracts and disciplined capacity expansion by leading providers.

Chart of the Week: since 30-Sep, software and large cap value valuations have improved, while semis and electronic and electrical equipment de-rated the most. Software and large cap value are the only groups that rose in valuation.

Batteries: demand is broadening beyond EVs into storage, data centres and physical AI. Next-generation chemistries (solid-state, sodium-ion, flow, metal-air, lithium-sulfur) are expected to complement lithium-ion rather than replace it, with adoption set by application-specific requirements.

Li-ion stays competitive for shorter-duration storage, but its economics weaken as duration rises. That creates openings for flow, metal-air, mechanical, thermal and other long-duration storage (LDES) solutions.

China sets the global battery cost curve through scale and integration. US and European policy is driving re-shoring but must overcome cost, execution and supply-chain constraints. Barclays identified about 80 public and private companies exposed to areas where batteries solve a binding infrastructure constraint.

New European systematic sector allocation framework: it converts US macro data into probabilities across six regimes (stress, stagflation, goldilocks, weakness, expansion, transition) and allocates across 35 European equity sectors monthly.

As of end-September 2026, expansion and transition were the two highest-probability regimes, keeping the model pro-cyclical. Cyclical exposure has come down from its 2025 peak, and the portfolio is overweight Industrials and Technology.

3Q26 US earnings season, week 1: 46 of 502 S&P 500 companies have reported, 78% beat on EPS (10Y median 79%) and 65% beat on sales. Blended EPS growth is 26.9% and blended revenue growth is 10.8%. A handful of bank misses made results mixed, but estimates keep rising and consumer checks are solid.

Europe strategy: surging oil is fueling inflation, social unrest and tighter credit conditions. Bonds are acting as safe havens again while equities are hit, but earnings and AI capex are holding up, so something has to give. Barclays flags PMIs, BigTech earnings and the FOMC next week.
Higher AI capex combined with higher rates is raising corporate financing costs. US tech IG yield and hyperscaler 12-month forward capex are both rising.

Credit strategy (Americas): AI credit is differentiating as issuer dispersion rises and curves steepen. The note also covers 2027 rising star and fallen angel outlook as the post-pandemic upgrade wave fades, and says SenFin underperformance looks stretched relative to cross-asset moves.

Credit (Europe): OATs, oil and AI funding concerns are the key drivers of credit volatility. Xover-5xMain has been range-bound despite OAT-Bund widening, which points to no systemic risk. Barclays expects widening risks to stay contained given stable growth, supportive yields and resilient market behaviour.

Asia credit: unwinds accelerated this week and Barclays keeps its 'use any bounce to de-risk' view. It favours short-dated (<2y) HY bonds with strong fundamentals, or high-quality long-duration/low-cash price bonds with more upside if rates stabilise or rally.

Rates: Treasuries are benefiting from a flight to safe havens on AI funding concerns. Barclays maintains receiving 1yf2y SOFR and recommends tactical 10s30s Treasury steepeners ahead of the QRA. In Japan, September saw the JGB curve bear-flatten.
EM strategy: EM credit is still decompressing while the market stays open for frontier sovereigns. Barclays sees more relative value in EM local and FX. Brazil faces a run-off election on Sunday.

Economic outlook: AI capex and oil worries are overriding solid corporate earnings. Higher energy costs and still-solid growth indicators imply more policy rate hikes, even if the Fed, ECB and BoJ stay on hold next week. Pressure on France increased.

earnings_insights: S&P 500 3Q26 scorecard: 46 of 502 companies have reported (11% of market cap). Reported EPS beat rate is 78% versus a 10Y median of 79%. Sales beat rate is 65%.

Blended EPS growth is 26.9% versus a 10Y median of 9.0%. Blended revenue growth is 10.8% versus a 10Y median of 5.6%. Blended combines estimates for companies yet to report with actuals for those that have.
Financials have reported 21 of 76 companies with a 48% revenue beat rate. Barclays notes a handful of bank misses made the start mixed.
Estimates continue moving higher and checks on the consumer remain solid. Results took a backseat to macro and AI last week, and prints should matter more as reporting market cap ramps up.
Upcoming company events: Thermo Fisher (TMO) post-Q3 investor meeting on 29 October and PPG post-earnings call on 29 October.
